title: The BMS Digital Library: a home for the movement's documents
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Books, resolutions, notices and photographs are being gathered in one searchable repository.
body:
A movement of seventy years leaves behind paper: conference reports, resolutions, memoranda, newsletters, books and photographs. Much of it is in boxes, in private collections or on unconnected websites. If it is not gathered and described, it is lost to the next generation of karyakartas and to researchers who want to understand India's labour history. This post explains the BMS Digital Library, what it is for and how members can help it grow.

## What the Digital Library is

BMS has set up a **Digital Library** on its .org domain, at *repository.bharatiyamazdoorsangh.org*, to gather such material in one place. The aim is to let karyakartas, researchers and students **find and read** documents without having to know where they are kept.

On a first visit, the site presents itself under the line "Nation first, Industry, Labour". It offers a search box that works in Hindi and English, and results can be viewed either as cards or as an index list. There is a login form, and the footer states that the content is view-only, with downloading and printing not permitted. That is a deliberate design choice and not a fault: it lets BMS make material available for reading while keeping control of how it circulates.

## Why a movement needs an archive

BMS was founded in Bhopal on 23 July 1955, and its own account says it began with no members, no office and no funds. Almost everything that came afterwards was recorded on paper at the time: the proceedings of its first all-India conference in 1967, when it counted 541 affiliated unions; its membership figures as verified by the Government in 1984 and 1996; its resolutions on wages, pensions and the Labour Codes; and the speeches and writings of its leaders. The V.V. Giri National Labour Institute, the Labour Ministry's research body, hosts a pamphlet titled *Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh at a Glance* and a presidential address to BMS's eighth national conference in Bangalore. These show that such documents already exist in public collections, but they are scattered. The same pamphlet lists periodicals, such as *Vishwakarma Chetna* in Hindi and *Vishwakarma Sanket* in English, and 24 books, which also need a permanent home.

There are practical reasons as well as historical ones. A trade union is constantly asked what it has said before. When a new Labour Code is discussed, the question may be what BMS demanded at the time of the earlier draft; when a minister says that a point was agreed, someone needs the original memorandum. A searchable record answers such questions faster than memory does. It also protects the organisation from the loss that follows when a long-serving office-bearer retires or an office is closed.

## What kinds of material belong in it

- **Conference reports and resolutions** of the all-India, State and federation conferences.
- **Memoranda and representations** submitted to governments, along with the replies, where they exist.
- **Circulars and notices** of the central office, States and federations.
- **Books, pamphlets and periodicals** published by BMS or by its research and training bodies.
- **Photographs** of meetings, rallies and leaders, with names and dates added.
- **Speeches and articles** of Dattopant Thengadi and others, some of which are already collected on the dbthengadi.in archive.

## How it relates to this website

- This portal, **bharatiyamazdoorsangh.com**, is the public face: news, leadership, press, gallery, blog and downloads.
- The **Digital Library** is the archive: documents and publications with metadata, meaning the date, author, subject and type of each item, so that a reader can find it later.

The official news site, bms.org.in, remains the place where current statements are first published. This website links to those statements, and the library keeps the older record.

## How you can help

- Send scans of **old notices, books and circulars** to the web team. Where possible, scan at a good quality, such as 300 dots per inch, keep pages in order, and write down who gave the item and when.
- Identify **people and dates** in old photographs. A photograph without a caption loses most of its value within one generation.
- Suggest **categories** that make browsing easier, whether by industry, State, theme or period.
- Tell the web team if an item is sensitive. Some papers may name individuals or relate to disputes, and should be checked before they are made public.
- Check the text. Where a document has been converted from a scan to searchable text, a careful reader can correct mistakes that the software has made, particularly in Hindi.

## Limits to keep in mind

A digital library holds copies, and a copy has to be handled with care. It is important to keep the original where it is safe. The library also reflects only what has been contributed; gaps in the record are gaps in what people have sent. Material is only as useful as its description, so each item should carry at least a title, a date and a source. And, as with any archive of a living organisation, the material shows BMS's own account of events. Researchers will want to compare it with Government records, newspapers and other unions' papers.

## Why archives matter

Organisations that remember do better than those that start from scratch each year. A library lets later generations learn from earlier ones. A young karyakarta preparing a memorandum on contract labour, for instance, can read what was said in an earlier decade, see what was achieved and what was not, and avoid repeating arguments that have already been tried. A student who wants to understand how an Indian union that is not tied to any party looked at economic reforms can read it in BMS's own words. And members who gave years of unpaid service can see that their work is recorded.
